parole.testo: Probably borrowed from Latin abissīnus (“Abyssinian”) or, alternatively, an internationalism (compare English Abyssinian, German Abessinier (“Abyssinian”), French Abyssin, Abyssinien (“Abyssinian”), abissino (“Abyssinian”)). Ultimately from Arabic حَبَشِيّ (ḥabašiyy, “Abyssinian”), from اَلْحَبَشَة
An internationalism either via German Abstraktion (“abstraction”) or directly from Latin abstractiō (“separation; abstraction”), from abstrahō (“I draw away, drag away”). With -ció ending.

parole.significato: an old liquid measure, about 50 liters
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Czech and Slovak okov or from Russian [Term?]. From Proto-Slavic *okovъ.
Most likely from Turkic, compare Old Turkic 𐰯𐰀 (pa /⁠apa⁠/, “father”), or from Proto-Uralic *ëppe (“father-in-law”).
Either from a South Slavic language, either Serbo-Croatian opàtica or Slovene opatica, or from Old High German appātissā. First attested in 1256.

Of debated origin: * Either from Proto-Uralic *šure- (“to cut, divide, distribute, share”), * or from a Turkic language, compare Proto-Turkic *or- and Ottoman Turkish اورامق (oramak). Either way, it is considered to have the Hungarian suffix -t and to be the variant of Hungarian irt, with which it u

parole.significato: Mason jar (glass jar with a screw top, often used for preserving food)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Romanian borcan (“jar”), of uncertain origin: an augmentative of boroacă (“swelling”); from Hungarian bokál (“pitcher”); or from Hungarian borkancsó (“wine pitcher”) or borkanna (“wine jug”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Of uncertain origin. Possibly related to the archaic bulya (“Turkish woman; concubine”), from Serbo-Croatian бу̏ла /bȕla (“a Muslim woman in harem pants or covered with a headscarf; a married woman”), from Ottoman Turkish بولا (bola, bula, “wife of one’s paternal uncle; lady, miss”). Alternatively,
From Old Turkic 𐰋𐰃𐰠 (b²il² /⁠bél⁠/, “waist”). Alternatively, perhaps from Proto-Uralic *pälɜ (“interior, inside”).

parole.significato: to confirm (to administer the sacrament of confirmation on someone)
parole.testo: From either Serbo-Croatian [Term?] or Slovene [Term?]. Compare Czech biřmovat and Polish bierzmować. First attested in 1519. With the verb-forming suffix -ál.

Borrowed from either Serbo-Croatian sirak or Slovene sirek, from Italian sorgo, from Latin (granum) syricum (“Syrian grain”). The word-initial consonant became affricated from sz to c. First attested in 1465.
Borrowed from either Bulgarian шипка (šipka, “rosehip”) or Slovak šípka (“rosehip”), from Proto-Slavic *šipъ (“thorn, spike”).

Two options: * either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ćolme (“knot, bundel; to bind”), cf. Hungarian csomó (“knot”), for the semantic shift cf. also German Knoten (“knot”) vs. Knochen (“bone”) (with a noun-forming suffix -t added in Hungarian, cf. evet, nyest, menyét, but the last three words might have a d

Probably a compound word. The first element is related to the base word of emse (“sow”) (originally meant “female”), which in turn is from Proto-Uralic *emä (“mother, woman”). The second element is either a variant of férj (“husband”) which originally meant “man” or is related to an unattested stem
Borrowed either from Italian eretico or French hérétique, from Latin hereticus, from Ancient Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikós, “able to choose”) + -nek (noun-forming suffix).

A Wanderwort, from a Romance language (e.g. French archiprêtre ← Old French archeprestre, Brescian Italian arsepret, Venetian Italian arsiprete) or from German Erzpriester; see more at English archpriest.
From Latin phoenīx, or from Ancient Greek φοῖνιξ (phoînix), from Egyptian bnw (boinu, “grey heron”).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak hrable. Compare Serbo-Croatian grablje.

parole.significato: garland (a decorative wreath or cord, used at festive occasions)
parole.testo: Either via German Girlande or French guirlande, from Italian ghirlanda (“garland”).
From an unattested stem + -öl. Alternatively, suggested to be a Turkic borrowing from Proto-Turkic *yǖl- (“to be mad, crazy; anger; to be sexually excited”).

parole.significato: dam (a structure placed across a flowing body of water to stop the flow or part of the flow)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, e.g. Serbo-Croatian gat, or from Slovak hať. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *gatь (“dike”).

parole.significato: gauze (a thin fabric with a loose, open weave used as a surgical dressing)
parole.testo: Either from German Gaze or French gaze, from Arabic قَزّ (qazz, “silk”).
Possibly from Proto-Uralic *kaja, or alternatively, from Proto-Uralic *koje. Possibly related to Finnish koi, Estonian koit and Erzya ки (ki).
According to Aikio (2016), from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kodwa (“short time, while”). Alternatively, from Proto-Finno-Ugric *kalɜ- (“to spend a night”).
From German ideal or from scientific Latin idealis. With -ális ending.
Either from Slovene kobilica (“locust”), from kobila (“mare”) or from Serbo-Croatian kobilica (“mare”).

parole.significato: ear, spike (the fruiting body of a grain plant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak klas, from Proto-Slavic *kolsъ.

parole.significato: Christmas; the feast day celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: Possibly a Bulgarian loanword, compare dialectal крачун (kračun, “winter solstice; a Slavic holiday celebrated at the winter solstice”), also compare dialectal Macedonian крачун (kračun, “Christmas”), Pannonian Rusyn Крачун (Kračun, “Christmas”), Slovak Kračún (“winter solstice feast”) (dialectal, "
Either from a Slavic language, compare kelih, or from German Kelch.

Likely from Oghur, from Proto-Turkic *koŋur; compare Chuvash хӑмӑр (hămăr). Alternatively, from an otherwise unattested stem of unknown origin + -r (nominal-forming suffix). It is also possible that it is a back-formation from komorodik or komorul.

parole.significato: comedy (dramatic work that is light and humorous or satirical in tone)
parole.testo: From Latin comoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía), from κῶμος (kômos, “revel, carousing”) + either ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) or ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer, bard”), both from ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”).
Borrowed from either a Serbo-Croatian kvar or Slovene kvar.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: leaf (thin, flattened organ of most vegetative plants)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Either derived from the same supposed stem as lebeg (“to float”); or from Proto-Ugric or perhaps Proto-Finno-Ugric *lᴕ̈pɜ, *lepɜ (“leaf”) (compare Erzya лопа (lopa, “leaf”)). The meaning “letter” is attested from the 14th century onwards.

parole.significato: county, shire (administrative region of a country)
parole.testo: Either from Serbo-Croatian međa (“border, boundary”) or Slovene meja (“border, boundary”). First attested in 1055.

parole.significato: master, craftsman (a tradesman who is qualified to teach apprentices)
parole.testo: First attested after 1372. Either via Old French maistre or Italian méster, from Latin magister (“teacher”).
Borrowed either from a South Slavic language or from Slovak mrena, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *merna. First attested in 1590.

Of debated origin. Either: # Borrowed from Alanic. Compare Ossetian марг (marg, “poison”). Further akin to Persian مرگ (marg, “death”). # From Proto-Finno-Ugric *mirkkɜ (“poison”). Compare Finnish myrkky (“poison”), but this is problematic.

First attested in 1811. Either from French mime (“pantomime actor”) or from German Mime, from Latin mimus (“mime actor”), from Ancient Greek μῖμος (mîmos, “imitator, actor”). With the verb-forming suffix -l. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries.

parole.significato: to skin (especially an animal) (to remove the skin and/or fur of)
parole.testo: The stem is of disputed origin: either from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńowe- (“to skin, flay”) (compare Proto-Samic *ńuovëtēk (“to skin”)) or from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńujɜ- (“to skin, flay”) (compare Udmurt [Term?] (“to skin”), Southern Mansi њо̄йөӈ (ńōjôň, “to skin”)). Formed with -z (frequentative verb-for

Inherited from Old Hungarian ollo, ollow (“kid (of a goat)”), which is borrowed from Danube Bulgar *oɣloŭ, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *oɣul-aɣ (“young of an animal”). The modern sense of "scissors" is apparently because scissor blades swing like a goat's legs. Alternatively, from obsolete sense "r

parole.significato: palette (a thin board on which a painter lays and mixes colours)
parole.testo: Either from French palette or German Palette.

parole.significato: cloak, mantle, robe, pall, cope (a long outer garment worn over the shoulders covering the back)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Bulgarian плащ (plašt) or from Serbo-Croatian plašt.

parole.significato: large-scale bribery, embezzlement or fraud, where an official provides an advantage to themselves or an associated pers…
parole.testo: Borrowed from German Panama (“financial scandal, bribery”) or from German Panama-Skandal (“Panama scandals”).

parole.significato: sling (an instrument for throwing stones or other missiles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Serbo-Croatian praća or Slovene práča, from Proto-Slavic *porťa (“sling”).

parole.significato: rat (a medium-sized rodent belonging to the genus Rattus)
parole.testo: A wanderword. Via either Slovene podgána or Italian pantegana. Compare Venetan pantegàna (“rat”). Ultimately from Byzantine Greek ποντικός (pontikós), from μῦς ποντικός (mûs pontikós, “rat”, literally “pontic mouse”).
From Old High German pehhari (“cup”), from Late Latin bicarium (“cup”), possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).

parole.significato: potbelly, paunch (the belly of a human, especially a large, fat protruding one)
parole.testo: Borrowed from either Russian потроха (potroxa) or Ukrainian потрохи (potroxy, “giblets”).
From Viennese German Strizzi (“rogue, pimp”), of uncertain origin, either from Czech strýc (“uncle”) or Italian strizzare (“to wring, squeeze”).

From either South Slavic or East Slavic, from Old Church Slavonic сѫбота (sǫbota), from Byzantine Greek *σάμβατον (*sámbaton), from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (šabbāṯ). The borrowing occurred in the eleventh century during the Christianization of the Hungarians, and befor

Uncertain. * Possibly from Proto-Finno-Ugric *śeppä (“skilled”) through Proto-Ugric *seppä. Hence also Proto-Samic *čeappē (“skillful”) and Proto-Finnic *seppä (“smith”). This explanation faces semantic difficulties. * Alternatively from a Turkic language, whence Chuvash шеп (šep, “beautiful”).
Of debated origin: * Borrowed either from Russian тележка (teležka) or from Ukrainian теліжка (teližka). * Derived from taliga (“barrow”) + -csa (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: interpreter (one who listens to a speaker in one language and relates that utterance to the audience in a different lan…
parole.testo: Borrowed either directly from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *tilmaç (“interpreter”) – Chuvash тӑлмач (tălmač, “interpreter”) –, or via a Slavic language, Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”).
Either from Italian tulipano or from Early New High German Tulipan (“tulip”), from Ottoman Turkish تولبند (tülbend), from Persian دلبند (dolband, “turban”)
Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak. Its original form was ugorka. Compare Slovak uhorka.

parole.significato: to practice magic, do things by magic
parole.testo: From a South Slavic language or from Slovak. Compare Serbo-Croatian vražiti⁽ˢʰ⁾ and Slovak vražiť (“to practice sorcery/magic/black art”), presumably from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ.

parole.significato: guest (a recipient of hospitality, specifically someone staying by invitation at the house of another)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Alanic *βændæg (“hostage, guest”). Alternatively, borrowed from Old Italian venedigo, venetico (“Venetian”).

parole.significato: to determine the direction in which someone or something proceeds
parole.testo: From Proto-Finno-Ugric *wetä-. Cognates include Finnish vetää. The Finno-Ugric root may be related to Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ-, either as loan or through genetic relationship.

From the same root as vezet (“to lead; drive”) + -ér (noun-forming suffix). The root is from Proto-Finno-Ugric *wetä- (“to lead, guide, draw, pull”). Cognates include Finnish vetää. The Finno-Ugric root may be related to Proto-Indo-European *wedʰ- (“to lead”), either as loan or through genetic relat

parole.significato: wax (a substance of animal or vegetable origin, consisting of fatty acids and alcohol, with a greasy sheen and feel, ma…
parole.testo: Either from Serbo-Croatian vosak (“wax”) or Slovene vosek (“wax”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *voskъ.
Borrowed either from Slovak or Ukrainian. Compare Slovak vaľok (“unburnt brick, adobe”), Ukrainian dialectal вальок (valʹok, “unburnt brick, adobe”).

parole.significato: branch (the woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing)
parole.testo: Of disputed origin. Either: * From Proto-Ugric *ϑaŋɜ (“branch, twig”). Cognates include Northern Mansi таг (tag, “twig, branch”). * From Proto-Finno-Ugric *šaŋka. Cognates include Finnish hanka.

parole.significato: to soak, steep (to be saturated with liquid by being immersed in it)
parole.testo: Of debated origin. Either from Proto-Ugric *ϑᴕćɜ- (“to become damp, get wet”) or from Proto-Finno-Ugric *sᴕsɜ- (“to become wet”) + -ik.
First attested in c. 1490. Of debated origin. Either from Proto-Finno-Ugric or Proto-Uralic *wᴕlmɜ (“lead”).

parole.significato: old (not young, having existed or lived for a long time; compare régi (“not new”))
parole.testo: From Proto-Ugric *üräŋɜ (“big, old”), whence also Proto-Khanty *ürǝɣ (> Northern Khanty ар (ar, “much, many”)) and Proto-Mansi *ärǝɣ (> Northern Mansi арыг (aryg, “extra, excess”)), derived from Proto-Uralic *ürä- (“big, old”) (whence Proto-Samoyedic *iräj (“grandfather”)). Alternatively, and less l

Of debated origin. Either from a Proto-Finno-Ugric stem + -öm (noun-forming suffix), or derived from a stem of Turkic origin, the same as in örül (“to be happy, rejoice”) and örvend (“to have pleasure, enjoy”).
